3D reference planes

Source: R/geom-plane-3d.R
geom_plane_3d.Rd

geom_plane_3d() draws planes clipped to the panel, such as reference planes at a fixed value of one variable, a fitted regression plane, or the planes of a system of linear equations. Like ggplot2::geom_hline(), it can draw planes given as parameters, or planes mapped from data.

Usage

geom_plane_3d(
  mapping = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  ...,
  xintercept,
  yintercept,
  zintercept,
  intercept,
  slope_x,
  slope_y,
  a,
  b,
  c,
  d,
  light = NULL,
  scale_depth = TRUE,
  on_top = FALSE,
  na.rm = FALSE,
  show.legend = NA,
  inherit.aes = FALSE
)

Arguments

mapping

Set of aesthetic mappings created by aes(), mapping the coefficients intercept, slope_x, and slope_y, or a, b, c, and d. Used only when no coefficients are given as parameters.

data

The data to be displayed in this layer.

...

Other arguments passed on to layer(), such as aesthetics like fill, alpha, colour (the outline, none by default), linewidth, and linetype.

xintercept, yintercept, zintercept

Positions of planes perpendicular to the x, y, or z axis.

intercept, slope_x, slope_y

Coefficients of regression planes z = intercept + slope_x * x + slope_y * y.

a, b, c, d

Coefficients of planes a * x + b * y + c * z = d.

light

A lighting specification object created by light(), light("none") or the string "none" to disable lighting, or NULL to inherit plot-level lighting. Set plot-level lighting by adding light() to the plot, and layer-specific lighting via the light argument of geom_*_3d() functions, which takes precedence.

scale_depth

Controls depth-based scaling, drawing closer elements larger or thicker and farther ones smaller or thinner. TRUE (the default) applies full scaling and FALSE disables it; a number sets the strength directly, where 1 matches TRUE, 0 matches FALSE, values below 1 subdue the effect and values above 1 exaggerate it. This affects the layer only; use coord_3d(scale_depth = ) for panel and axis components.

on_top

If TRUE, the layer is drawn on top of the rest of the scene instead of being depth-sorted with it, so other geometry never hides or cuts it, e.g. to keep labels legible. The layers drawn on top are depth-sorted among themselves. Default FALSE.

na.rm

If FALSE, planes with missing coefficients are removed with a warning.

show.legend

Logical indicating whether this layer should be included in legends. Planes given as parameters are never included.

inherit.aes

If TRUE, combine the plot's default aesthetics with mapping. Defaults to FALSE, since planes rarely share the plot's aesthetics.

Value

A ggplot2 layer.

Plane forms

Planes can be given in one of three forms:

  • xintercept, yintercept, or zintercept: planes perpendicular to an axis, e.g. yintercept = 2 for the plane y = 2. Only one of the three can be used per layer. This form can only be given as parameters, not mapped, since it would otherwise affect the axis's range.

  • intercept, slope_x, slope_y: the plane z = intercept + slope_x * x + slope_y * y, as from a linear model. Any of the three left out defaults to 0.

  • a, b, c, d: the general form a * x + b * y + c * z = d. Requires a, b, and c (not all zero); d defaults to 0.

Given as parameters, values can be vectors to draw several planes, along with styling parameters of the same length. In the general form, for example, a, b, c can be the columns of a matrix A and d the right-hand side of the linear system A x = d. To draw planes from a data frame instead, map the coefficients of the regression or general form in aes(). Each layer uses one form.

Rendering

Planes are built from the panel's limits when the plot is drawn, so they don't expand the plot's axis ranges; a plane that misses the panel entirely is skipped with a warning. They are depth-sorted with the rest of the scene, split where they intersect other polygons, lit from whichever side faces the viewer, and never removed by back-face culling. Points, segments, lines, and text lying exactly in a plane are drawn on top of it.

Coefficients are in the plot's (transformed) scale space: with scale_x_log10(), for example, xintercept = 2 is the plane at x = 100.

Aesthetics

geom_plane_3d() understands the following aesthetics: a, b, c, d, intercept, slope_x, slope_y (see above), fill, alpha, colour, linewidth, and linetype.

Examples

# Reference planes through a point cloud
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, hp, mpg)) +
  geom_point_3d() +
  coord_3d(yaw = 120)
p + geom_plane_3d(zintercept = 20)


# A fitted regression plane
fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
b <- coef(fit)
p + geom_plane_3d(intercept = b[1], slope_x = b["wt"], slope_y = b["hp"],
                  fill = "steelblue")


# The planes of a linear system, meeting at its solution
A <- rbind(c(1, 1, 1), c(1, -1, 0), c(0, 1, -1))
ggplot() +
  geom_plane_3d(a = A[, 1], b = A[, 2], c = A[, 3], d = c(1, 0, 0),
                fill = c("tomato", "seagreen", "steelblue")) +
  geom_point_3d(aes(x, y, z), data = data.frame(x = 1/3, y = 1/3, z = 1/3),
                size = 3) +
  lims(x = c(-1, 1), y = c(-1, 1)) + zlim(-1, 1) +
  coord_3d()


# Planes mapped from data, with a fill scale
planes <- data.frame(slope_x = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5), model = c("a", "b", "c"))
ggplot() +
  geom_plane_3d(aes(slope_x = slope_x, fill = model), data = planes) +
  lims(x = c(-1, 1), y = c(-1, 1)) + zlim(-1, 1) +
  coord_3d()
